book_long_title: Laxman Sen: The Rise of the Last Great Sena
target_audience: general public, students of history and literature
book_summary: Laxman Sen is remembered by history as a weak king — the man who lost Bengal to Bakhtiyar Khalji. But before the fall, there was a rise. A prince of the Sena line, born to the dream of his father Ballala Sena, marched north to the heart of Aryavarta, planted the Sena banner on the walls of Kannauj, and returned to sit upon the throne of Gauda as the greatest patron of learning Bengal had ever known. He gathered at his court the poets Jayadeva, Halayudha, Dhoyi, Govardhana, Umapatidhara, and Sharan, and in that golden age the Gita Govinda was written. But while he gathered poets, a shadow was gathering in the west — Bakhtiyar Khalji, who fell upon Nabadwip by surprise in 1203–04 and ended the age. Laxman Sen fled east to Vikrampur, and died a king without a capital. Yet the Gita Govinda survived, and the name of the king who lost Bengal survived too — not as a conqueror, but as a patron. History remembers him as weak; the poets remember him as great. This is the story of the rise, and the shadow the rise cast.
gist: A prince of the Sena line marches north to plant the Sena banner on the walls of Kannauj, returns to sit upon the throne of Gauda as Bengal's greatest patron of learning, and must face the shadow riding down from the mountains of the west.

chapters.name: The Seed
chapters.chapter_summary: The Sena line comes north out of the Karnata country, and Vijaya Sena sharpens the Sena blade against the soft Pala empire. Ballala Sena, the lawgiver, dreams of the north, and into that dream his son Lakshmana is born — with a prophecy that he will rise higher and fall further than any Sena.

chapters.name: The Forging
chapters.chapter_summary: The boy Laxman grows in the palace at Vikrampur, learning the Vedas, the sword, and statecraft — and learning to listen. The old king lays the dream before him: take Kannauj, plant the Sena banner in the north.

chapters.name: The Conquest
chapters.chapter_summary: The army of Bengal crosses the Ganga and marches north through Magadha and Mithila, past the ruins of Pataliputra and the holy city of Kashi, to the walls of Kannauj, where the Gahadavala king Jayachandra waits.

chapters.name: The Crown
chapters.chapter_summary: The battle for Kannauj is long and terrible, and Laxman Sen fights in the thick of it. The Gahadavala line breaks, the city falls, and the Sena banner is planted on the highest tower. He raises victory pillars across the doab, then turns south toward home.

chapters.name: The Golden Age
chapters.chapter_summary: Ballala Sena dies before his son returns. Laxman Sen is crowned at Nabadwip, and turns from the sword to the pen, gathering the greatest poets of the age — Jayadeva, Halayudha, Dhoyi, Govardhana — and the Gita Govinda is written in his court.

chapters.name: The Shadow
chapters.chapter_summary: While Laxman Sen gathers poets, Bakhtiyar Khalji rides out of the west. In 1203–04 he falls upon Nabadwip by surprise, and the golden age ends in a single night of fire and blood. Laxman Sen flees east to Vikrampur.

chapters.name: The Echo
chapters.chapter_summary: Laxman Sen dies around 1206, a king without a capital. But the Gita Govinda survives, and the name of the king who lost Bengal survives too — not as a conqueror, but as a patron. History remembers him as weak; the poets remember him as great.
